name: Idebenone

card.summary: A synthetic coenzyme Q10 analog used as an antioxidant ingredient in anti-aging skincare and as a prescription drug for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy.
card.note: Cosmetic effects are less studied than its medical uses.

quick.overview:
Idebenone is a synthetic quinone resembling coenzyme Q10. In skincare it is marketed as a strong antioxidant for reducing the look of fine lines and wrinkles.

Its best-studied use is medical: it is approved in the EU as Raxone for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), and the LEROS trial reported long-term vision benefits. Wikipedia notes clinical evidence for the anti-wrinkle use is lacking.
quick.how: In cosmetics it appears in topical serums and creams applied to skin. Medical use is by prescription in tablet form.
quick.risks: Topical use is generally described as well tolerated. Prescription idebenone is medically supervised, and some other approvals have been withdrawn after trials failed to show efficacy.

lead: Idebenone is a synthetic analog of coenzyme Q10 in the quinone family, sold as Raxone, Catena and Sovrima [1]. It has a shorter side chain than CoQ10, which Grokipedia says makes it more water-soluble and better at crossing membranes [2]. In cell and tissue models it acts as a mitochondrial electron carrier and inhibits lipid peroxidation, although its clinical relevance has not been established [1].

For appearance, it is an ingredient in topical anti-aging products, marketed as an antioxidant that helps with the look of fine lines and wrinkles. Users apply serums or creams to the face expecting smoother-looking skin over time, [1][2]. Wikipedia states that clinical evidence for the wrinkle use is lacking [1].

Its medical history is separate and better documented. It was developed by Takeda for Alzheimer disease and cognitive disorders, later pursued by Santhera for neuromuscular and eye conditions, and is authorised in the EU as Raxone for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), where the pivotal and follow-up trials were run [1][5][6].

angle.text: Skincare brands include idebenone for its antioxidant, CoQ10-like action, with users aiming at fewer visible fine lines. Published trials focus on eye and neuromuscular disease.

infobox: Takeda; later Santhera; Chiesi holds the EU authorisation

paras: Topical idebenone appears in anti-wrinkle products as an antioxidant [1]. Grokipedia says topical formulations have been developed for anti-aging and protection against UV-induced skin damage, citing the compound's stability and low irritation, and that research is looking at delivery systems because systemic absorption by mouth is limited [2]. No published clinical trial of idebenone skincare has been identified; proponents' reasoning rests on its antioxidant action seen in lab models [1][2].

LHON is an inherited mitochondrial disease causing rapid, severe vision loss in both eyes, and is estimated to be the most frequent mitochondrial disease [3]. The European Commission authorised Raxone for visual impairment in people aged 12 and over with LHON on 8 September 2015, under exceptional circumstances, after a positive CHMP opinion in June 2015; it is prescription-only, with treatment supervised by a doctor experienced in LHON, and the company must keep a registry and run long-term safety studies [7]. The orphan designation dates from 2007 and ended in September 2025 when market exclusivity expired [1][7]. A consensus statement discusses uncertainty about the best timing and population for treatment [3]. Common side effects listed by the EMA include nasopharyngitis and cough, with diarrhoea and back pain less often [7].

Japan approved idebenone in 1986 for cognitive and behavioural symptoms of dementia, marketed by Takeda as Avan, and withdrew the approval in 1998 [1][2]. Canada gave conditional approval for Friedreich ataxia in 2008, followed by a voluntary recall in 2013 after further trials did not show efficacy; the EMA had refused approval for that use in 2008 [1]. In Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a phase III trial reported reduced decline in respiratory function [8], and long-term data on respiratory outcomes have been published [9]; a later trial in glucocorticoid-treated patients did not repeat the benefit, and no approval followed, according to Grokipedia [2]. Trials in MELAS and in multiple sclerosis have also been run [1].

Oral bioavailability is under 1 percent because of first-pass metabolism; more than 99 percent is protein bound, the elimination half-life is about 18 hours, and about 80 percent is excreted in urine [1]. Laboratory work has shown that it can carry electrons directly to complex III, bypassing complex I defects, and scavenge reactive oxygen species [2]. A 2024 preclinical study reported that idebenone reduced doxorubicin-induced heart toxicity in models by stabilising FSP1 to inhibit ferroptosis [10].

The LEROS open-label trial (199 patients, matched natural-history control of 372) found that idebenone treatment confirmed long-term efficacy in LHON up to five years after symptom onset, with effects varying by disease phase and mutation [4]. Early work in Friedreich ataxia included a 2002 trial in early-stage patients and a 2008 survey of antioxidant use in the disease [11][12]. Reviews of mitochondrial optic neuropathies and ataxia treatments place idebenone among the agents examined [13][14].
No studies found of cosmetic topical use.

It is prescription-only where approved. Brand names include Raxone, Catena, Sovrima and Avan [1][2]. Grokipedia reports that in the United States idebenone is not approved for LHON or any other indication, and that a new drug application from Chiesi was under FDA review [2]. Cosmetic products containing idebenone are sold without prescription in many markets [1].

timeline.event: Japan approves idebenone (Avan) for dementia-related symptoms [2].
Canada grants conditional approval for Friedreich ataxia; EMA refuses that use [1][2].
Health Canada recall of Sovrima/Catena after trials fail to show efficacy [1].
European Commission authorises Raxone for LHON on 8 September [7].
LEROS trial publishes long-term LHON results [4].
Orphan designation expires in the EU after 10-year exclusivity [7].
